video_subject: How dolphins sleep with half their brain
video_script: Dolphins never fully fall asleep. If they did, they could drown. Every breath a dolphin takes is a conscious decision, so it can't just switch off like we do. Instead, it sleeps with half of its brain at a time. One side rests while the other side stays awake, keeps it swimming, and brings it up to breathe. The eye on the awake side stays open, watching for sharks and keeping track of the pod. A few hours later, the two halves swap. Scientists call this unihemispheric sleep. In one study, dolphins stayed alert and kept echolocating for five days straight with no sign of getting tired. So the next time you hit snooze, remember: somewhere in the ocean, a dolphin is napping with one eye open. Follow for a new dolphin fact every day.

Dolphins have names. Not words like ours, but something very close. In its first few months of life, every bottlenose dolphin invents its own signature whistle, a unique sound that works like a name. Other dolphins learn it, and they copy it when they want to call that specific individual. When researchers played a dolphin's signature whistle through an underwater speaker, that dolphin answered, while the others mostly ignored it. It gets even better. Dolphins seem to remember the whistles of old companions for more than twenty years, even after living apart. That is the longest social memory ever measured in an animal other than humans. So when you hear a pod chattering, they may be calling each other by name. Follow for a new dolphin fact every day.

video_subject: Echolocation: how dolphins see with sound
video_script: Dolphins can see with sound. It's called echolocation. A dolphin makes rapid clicks inside its head, and a fatty organ in its forehead, called the melon, focuses them into a beam. When the clicks hit something, they bounce back. The dolphin picks up those echoes through its lower jaw, which carries the sound to its inner ear. From that echo, its brain works out an object's size, shape, distance, and even what it's made of. Dolphins can find fish hiding under sand and pick out a target in murky water where their eyes are useless. Some clicks are so fast they blend into a buzz as the dolphin closes in on its prey. Imagine shouting into the dark and getting back a picture. That's every day for a dolphin. Follow for a new dolphin fact every day.

Spinner dolphins are the acrobats of the ocean. They launch out of the water and twist around as many as seven times in a single leap before crashing back down. Why do they do it? Scientists have a few ideas. The huge splash makes a sound that travels underwater, so spinning might be a way to signal the rest of the pod. It may also help shake off clinging fish called remoras. And sometimes, it just looks like play. Spinner dolphins live in big groups, sometimes hundreds strong. They rest in calm, shallow bays during the day and head out into deep water at night to hunt small fish and squid. Then the sun comes up, and the show begins again. Follow for a new dolphin fact every day.

The killer whale isn't a whale at all. It's a dolphin, the biggest one on the planet. Orcas belong to the same family as the bottlenose dolphin, and adult males can grow more than eight meters long and weigh around six tonnes. Their families are run by females. Calves often stay with their mothers for life, and grandmothers, who can live past eighty, lead the group to food in hard times. Different orca populations speak different dialects and specialize in different prey. Some eat only fish. Others hunt seals or even whales. They work together like a team, with techniques passed down from one generation to the next. Smart, social, and a little terrifying, the orca is the ultimate dolphin. Follow for a new dolphin fact every day.

Some dolphins use tools. In Shark Bay, Australia, a group of bottlenose dolphins tears marine sponges off the sea floor and wears them on their beaks. Why? They hunt fish hiding in the rough, rocky bottom, and the sponge works like a glove, protecting their snouts as they dig. This trick, called sponging, isn't instinct. It's learned. Calves pick it up by watching their mothers, and it's mostly passed from mothers to daughters. That makes it one of the clearest examples of culture in any wild animal. The same population has another trick too. Some dolphins chase fish into large empty seashells, lift the shell above the surface, and shake the fish into their mouths. Clever doesn't even begin to cover it. Follow for a new dolphin fact every day.

A baby dolphin is usually born tail first. That helps keep it from drowning during birth. The moment it arrives, its mother, and sometimes another female from the pod, guides it up to the surface for its very first breath. Newborn calves have soft fins and faint folds on their sides from being curled up in the womb. For the first month, something amazing happens. Mother and calf barely rest at all, staying on the move almost nonstop. The calf drinks milk that's very rich in fat, and it may keep nursing for two years or more. It will stay by its mother's side for three to six years, learning how to hunt, where to find food, and who's who in the pod. Dolphin moms are some of the most devoted in the ocean. Follow for a new dolphin fact every day.

video_subject: The pink dolphins of the Amazon
video_script: There are pink dolphins in the Amazon River. They're called botos, or Amazon river dolphins, and they're the largest river dolphins in the world. Babies are born gray. They tend to turn pink as they get older, and the males are often the pinkest, partly because of scar tissue from fighting. Unlike ocean dolphins, the bones in their necks aren't fused, so they can turn their heads from side to side. That flexibility comes in handy. Every rainy season the river floods the rainforest, and botos swim between the trunks of submerged trees, hunting fish among the roots. But they're in trouble. Botos are listed as endangered, threatened by dams, pollution, and fishing nets. Protect the river, and you protect the pink dolphin. Follow for a new dolphin fact every day.

Dolphins breathe through the top of their heads. That's the blowhole, and it's really a nostril that moved during evolution. It stays sealed by a muscular flap underwater and opens only when the dolphin reaches the surface. A dolphin's airway isn't connected to its mouth, so it can catch fish without ever getting water in its lungs. Each breath is incredibly efficient. In a quick exhale and inhale, a dolphin can refresh around eighty percent of the air in its lungs. We swap out only a small fraction of ours. That's how it can stay underwater for several minutes and dive deep. And remember, every one of those breaths is a choice. A dolphin has to think to breathe. Follow for a new dolphin fact every day.

video_subject: Dolphins recognize themselves in a mirror
video_script: Dolphins can recognize themselves in a mirror. That might sound simple, but very few animals can do it. In a famous experiment, scientists put a harmless mark on a dolphin's body, somewhere it could only see in a reflection. The dolphin swam straight to the mirror and twisted around to inspect the mark. It knew the dolphin in the glass was itself. Since then, researchers have found that young dolphins start showing this kind of self-awareness at around seven months old. Human babies usually don't pass the mirror test until they're about a year and a half. Only a handful of other animals, like great apes, elephants, and magpies, have shown signs of it. Dolphins aren't just smart. They know who they are. Follow for a new dolphin fact every day.
